chunks: With this chain of transmission, from al-Ḥusayn ibn Saʿīd, from ʿUthmān ibn ʿĪsā, from Samāʿah, who said:
I asked him about the urine of a boy that affects a garment, and he said: “Wash it.” I said: “What if I do not find its place?” He said: “Wash the entire garment.”

Then he said—may Allah, the Exalted, support him: There is no harm in the sweat of a menstruating woman and the junub, and washing the garment because of it is not obligatory, unless the janabah is from what is haram; then he should wash whatever the sweat of its possessor has affected, whether of body or garment, and he should act with precaution regarding taharah. What he informed me of indicates this.

key_terms.اغْسِلْهُ: wash it; the command to cleanse the affected area
key_terms.الثَّوْبَ: the garment or clothing that requires purification
key_terms.الطَّهَارَةِ: ritual purity and the rules governing purification
key_terms.الْجَنَابَةُ: the state of major ritual impurity
key_terms.الْجُنُبِ: a person in the state of janabah
key_terms.بَوْلِ الصَّبِيِّ: the urine of a young boy affecting a garment
key_terms.حَرَامٍ: that which is forbidden, here qualifying the cause of janabah

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on a child’s urine on clothing, and does the sweat of a menstruating woman or junub make clothes impure?
ai.summary: This hadith gives a legal ruling on purifying clothing affected by najasah, specifically the urine of a child: if the exact spot is known it should be washed, and if it is unknown the whole garment should be washed. It also states that the sweat of a menstruating woman and a junub is not problematic in itself, except in the case of janabah from what is haram, where precaution in taharah and washing what was affected is required.
